extracted.intended_audience: artists, critics, and general readers interested in aesthetics and how to judge or produce art
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging and producing ‘true’ art, emphasising infectiousness, subject-matter, universality, simplicity, and moral ('religious') perception; guidance aimed at artists and critics on what counts as art versus counterfeits. Uses examples (Dickens, Romeo and Juliet, folk-stories) to illustrate tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art unites men; subject-matter must serve well-being
rubrics_metrics.description: Art unites men. Surely it is desirable that the feelings in which it unites them should be 'the best and highest to which men have risen,' or at least should not run contrary to our perception of what makes for the well-being of ourselves and of others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy's 'religious perception' defines what makes for well-being; art should promote feelings that foster brotherhood, love, and compassion rather than feelings that hinder human well-being.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two kinds of legitimate subject-matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Therefore the subject-matter of what we, in our day, can esteem as being the best art, can be of two kinds only—(1) Feelings flowing from the highest perception now attainable by man ... (2) The simple feelings of common life, accessible to every one—provided that they are such as do not hinder progress towards well-being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: (1) Dickens' 'Christmas Carol' (compassion and love) as highest-perception art; (2) folk-stories, nursery rhymes, harmless jokes and even dolls, provided they transmit wholesome feelings and do not impede moral progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infectiousness as the sign of art
rubrics_metrics.description: The sign of art: infectiousness — it 'infects' others with the feeling of the artist; art must transmit feeling and unite author and audience in feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A work that 'infects' binds people together in common feeling; if a work merely interests, effects, or amazes without infecting, it is not true art. Assess whether the reader/viewer genuinely shares the feeling transmitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality / comprehensibility to normal people
rubrics_metrics.description: What fails to infect normal people is not art. The highest art has always been comprehensible to normal people; art should be universal rather than 'exclusive'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test works by how widely they can spread and the classes they reach: a universal work (e.g., the story of Joseph) reaches masses across time and cultures; 'exclusive art' infects only a trained minority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions of infection: individuality, clearness, sincerity
rubrics_metrics.description: Conditions of infection: Individuality; Clearness; Sincerity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A work must express the artist's individual feeling clearly and sincerely to infect others; technical virtuosity or ornament without sincere individuality will fail to transmit feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge art by the feelings it transmits, not by deduced moral
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the feelings with which you are infected when reading, and not any moral you can deduce, that is subject-matter of art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not excuse harmful subject-matter because a reader can draw a moral afterward; the immediate feeling infection is the relevant evaluative criterion (Romeo and Juliet transmits sensual attraction even if its plot yields disastrous consequences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and compression necessary for universal art
rubrics_metrics.description: It has not the 'simplicity and compression' necessary in works of 'universal' art. ... The style, also, is not one of great simplicity; the sentences are often long and involved ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Universal art tends toward clear, simple, compressed expression; excess detail, locality, and convoluted sentences make a work 'exclusive' and limit its infectious reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty is not a defining criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: For beauty (i.e., 'that which pleases')—though it depends on taste, and can furnish no criterion for art—will be a natural characteristic of work done, not for hire, nor even for fame, but because men ... wish to share ... spiritual strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beauty (pleasing form) may accompany genuine art but cannot alone define it; focus evaluation on transmitted feeling and moral quality rather than merely pleasing aesthetics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art's moral/subject-matter must not be harmful
rubrics_metrics.description: But how are we to know what are the 'best' feelings? What is good? and what is evil? This is decided by 'religious perception' ... Our religious perception ... is the consciousness that our well-being ... lies in the growth of brotherhood among men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject subject-matter that promotes patriotism as preference for one's country leading to war, sectarian church divisions, sensuality, or other feelings that obstruct brotherhood and well-being.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive art vs. universal art
rubrics_metrics.description: Either they fail to infect ... or they are works of 'exclusive art,' bad in form and capable of infecting only a select audience trained and habituated to such inferior art; or they are bad in subject-matter...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of works that require special education or habituation ('the elect') to be moved; such exclusivity disqualifies them from highest art even if technically masterful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterfeits of art: borrowing, imitating, striking, interesting
rubrics_metrics.description: Counterfeits of art produced by: Borrowing; Imitating; Striking; Interesting—Qualifications needful for production of real works of art, and those sufficient for production of counterfeits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A work that merely borrows, imitates, or seeks to be striking/merely interesting may attract attention but lacks infectious sincerity. Identify whether a work's appeal is genuine feeling or mere effect/novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of counterfeits: professionalism, criticism, schools
rubrics_metrics.description: Causes of production of counterfeits—Professionalism—Criticism—Schools of art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professionalisation, self-perpetuating schools, and critical fashions can encourage art that prioritises technique, market, or reputation over sincere feeling; consider institutional incentives when assessing authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent/spread of a work indicates its effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The more widely they are spread the greater will be their effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure a work's significance partly by how broadly it unites people in the transmitted feeling across social strata, times, and places (e.g., folk-stories vs. elite drama).

rubrics_metrics.name: Art should transform perception into feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Art should transform this perception into feeling. The destiny of art in our time is to transmit from the realm of reason to the realm of feeling the truth that well-being for men consists in being united together ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artists should convert rational insights about human well-being into feelings that can be shared and felt by others; art's role is emotional transmission of ethical truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art is progressive; subject-matter improves with moral perception
rubrics_metrics.description: One result ... is that art is not stationary but progressive. ... We must no longer esteem as good in subject-matter poems which appeal to the Eternal to destroy a man's private or national foes; for we have reached a 'religious perception' which bids us have no foes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate historical works in light of current moral perception: subject-matter once acceptable may now be judged inferior because it conflicts with improved ethical understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility and cost: art must be for all
rubrics_metrics.description: Our art too expensive, too unintelligible, and too harmful for the masses ... Real art needful for all men ... The art of the future not a possession of a select minority, but a means towards perfection and unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a work is accessible (intellectually and materially) to common people; art that is prohibitively expensive or intelligible only to a leisure class is failing its social purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style qualities expected: clearness, beauty, simplicity, compression
rubrics_metrics.description: With so much to say ... the art of the future will, in matter of form also, be far superior to our art in 'clearness, beauty, simplicity, and compression' (p. 194).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical stylistic guidance for creators: aim for clear, simple, compressed expression that aids infectious transmission of feeling rather than ornate convolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test works by internal test of feelings transmitted
rubrics_metrics.description: He does not deny that it is a work of art, that it infects ... but what are the feelings it transmits? That is to say, judging by the internal test, Tolstoy admits that Romeo and Juliet unites him to its author and to other people in feeling. But the work is very far from being one of 'universal' art ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the 'internal test' — identify the actual feelings transmitted to the audience (e.g., sensual attraction in Romeo and Juliet) and evaluate whether those feelings are desirable or harmful to human well-being.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical virtuosity or realism do not equal art
rubrics_metrics.description: Tried by such tests, the enormous majority of the things we have been taught to consider great works of art are found wanting. Either they fail to infect (and attract merely by being interesting, realistic, effectful, or by borrowing from others), ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between technical skill, realism, novelty, or cleverness and genuine infectious feeling; any of the former without the latter should be considered a counterfeit or inferior art.
